text.p: Deutsche Bank AG, Germany's largest bank, on Thursday reported a nine percent rise in group net income in the first nine months of 1996, marking a slowdown from 15 percent growth in the first half of the year.

Group net profit rose to 1.5 billion marks from 1.4 billion marks while operating profit jumped 25.8 percent to 3.49 billion marks, the bank said in its interim report. The results were broadly in line with expectations.

Analysts said the slowdown was caused by an acceleration in administration costs during the third quarter as Deutsche continued to throw money at its expanding investment bank business, concentrated at London unit Morgan Grenfell.

Net earnings were also restrained by a sharp rise in taxes to 1.5 billion marks from 1.0 billion and by the cost of bailing out Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM), hit by irregularities at three unit trusts.

But Deutsche's profit growth was buoyant nonetheless, driven by a 46.6 percent surge in trading income to 2.1 billion marks as financial markets continued to rise. That level exceeded its entire 1995 trading profit of 2.0 billion marks.

Net commission income rose 25.9 percent to 4.9 billion marks, a slight slowdown from 29.5 percent growth in the first half which was in keeping with the usual summer lull in July and August, analysts said.
The gains pushed Deutsche's return on equity to 14.3 percent before tax from 12.4 percent, still a long way off the bank's long-term goal of 25 percent.
Administration costs climbed 10 percent to 10.9 billion marks after rising 7.7 percent in the first six months.
"The main factor behind the earnings slowdown was the increasing momentum of administration costs," said Dieter Hein, banking analyst at BHF Bank AG in Frankfurt.
Risk provisions for loan losses rose to 1.2 billion marks from 1.0 billion, while net interest income after risk provisions edged down 0.9 percent to 6.8 billion marks.

It was an eventful third quarter for Deutsche which dominated headlines with news of a management revamp, the announcement it had a stake in rival Bayerische Vereinsbank, the fiasco at MGAM, and speculation that it may lose its prized Aaa credit rating.
Deutsche injected a net 180 million pounds into MGAM after irregularities in the running of three unit trusts came to light in September.
But analysts said the MGAM affair, which led to the departure of four key managers at the asset management group, had hurt Deutsche's image more than its pocket.
Hein at BHF Bank estimated the affair cost Deutsche 150 to 250 million marks in the third quarter and said it was unclear whether fourth-quarter results would be affected as well.

Deutsche made no comment on the MGAM affair in its interim report, which coincided with an article in the Financial Times that MGAM was in danger of losing a 200 million pounds sterling mandate to manage pension funds for a London council.

"The report suggests the problem has spread to the pensions business and that is a real problem," said Matthew Czepliewicz, banking analyst at Salomon Brothers in London. But Deutsche's earnings would not be affected, he added.

Several analysts said they would probably cut their earnings forecasts for Deutsche in 1996 and saw earnings under pressure at most European banks from an expected downturn in financial markets in 1997.
Hein at BHF Bank said he may lower his forecast for 1996 net profit per share from his current prediction of 4.40 marks.

Group lending grew by 20.7 billion marks to 400 billion marks. The balance sheet total advanced strongly by 21.8 percent to 879.1 billion marks due to increased activities in its investment banking business.

Deutsche's shares rose as much as one percent to a day's high of 71.92 marks in pre-bourse after the results, but slipped during floor trade to close at 71.45 marks, down 12 pfennigs. The shares outperformed the overall market.
